title_original: Ryusuke Hamaguchi on All of a Sudden, His American Debut, and Embracing the Impossible

blocks.text: There was a very possible path for Ryusuke Hamaguchi that would’ve gone poorly. The small class of international auteurs who achieve such a level of success as Drive My Car swiftly find themselves courted by entities who will bring them into the whirlpool of international co-productions or, God help them, American studio films that stifle their instincts while stealing years of life. Evil Does Not Exist did effectively nothing to match anticipation over a follow-up, which is not even accounting for that film streamlining its initial iteration: a silent film with live-scoring .

All of a Sudden , by nature of support from Japanese and French entities, comes closer to the co-production I’m describing; that’s about where conforming to standards ends. A lengthy, verbose, discursive project that commingles elder care, capitalist critique, and—returning Hamaguchi to his roots—experimental theater, the film has been subject of our praise since its Cannes premiere in May, since which it’s been awarded the Indie Film Site Network’s Advocate Award (other commendations from other groups are most likely coming, but if not, that’ll have to do). With Hamaguchi in town during All of a Sudden ‘s New York Film Festival premiere, I was happy to catch up with a filmmaker I’ve been admiring (and occasionally distributing) since 2016, a time when this level of success was frankly impossible to envision.
My thanks to Aiko Masubuchi for providing interpretation.

The Film Stage: To what extent are you accounting for light, be it natural or artificial, being different between Japan and France, or an atmosphere created by architecture? How much are you grappling with it, and how much are you leaning in?

Ryusuke Hamaguchi: I think that ultimately happens whether I want to or not, just because, ultimately, the areas within the vicinity of where I live—the 200-meter radius of where I live, or places I know intimately, to the point where I know where the alleys are, where certain things are—I try to avoid making films in the area that I live in. So if I were to make a film there, I would know exactly where to place the camera in order to create a shot. For example: when I was making Intimacies , I’d already been living in Tokyo for about 10 years at that point, so—again—I knew exactly where I wanted to position my camera. We didn’t really have a big budget at that time, but I knew if I placed a camera here, I could make a film. But now, with this film, I was working somewhere where I had no personal history. For that reason, I didn’t know where I couldn’t really place the camera, so I was feeling a little wary about that.

But I would say maybe 70 to 80% of the film happens inside—especially within the care facility—and in terms of thinking about where else we were going to shoot, we had set the care facility to be in the outskirts of Paris, so that’s where we were looking. But I knew that I didn’t want images that were “postcard images”—I didn’t want the Eiffel Tower, for instance, as part of the image. What I really wanted was the perspective of someone who actually lives in Paris, so I talked to the assistant directors who live in Paris and asked them about their favorite locations. There’s a park called the Chapeau-Rouge, which is one of the places where we ended up shooting, and there’s a terrace on the National Library. Again: even when we did shoot on the Seine, we weren’t shooting somewhere that was close to the Eiffel Tower. So it was places that people who live there know about.

One thing I tried to think about is to not add anything through the image. And what I mean by that is: I use a very standard lens and I don’t try to make anywhere look “more beautiful” than how it is. If it looks good already, I will try to shoot as is. I think perhaps, through that, you get the sense, as you said, of the atmosphere of the place. And I’m not really thinking about whether that in itself really helps or doesn’t help the storytelling, but something that I am always thinking about is Bresson’s words, which says that the face of the model should not be eaten up by the background. So I think, because of that, you don’t emphasize the background as much, and I think perhaps through that you get a sense of the atmosphere of the place.
Across the three hours, the moment that amazed me most was when they’re sitting outside in Japan and we get what you could call the Tarkovsky / Mirror shot.
A-ha.

And in the far distance, as the sun is rising, we see this car’s headlights pass right between the two of them. Was that planned as part of the composition? And if it wasn’t, how much is it then about this conscious decision of: you shoot ten takes, then you want this one that has an extra moment of life to it? Does it then become this necessity that this moment be included because it gets at the idea of things happening around us?

I’m embarrassed to admit that I’ve actually never seen Mirror by Tarkovsky. [Laughs] So if that shot is similar, then I guess I’m very grateful that it is, but I’m embarrassed to say I’ve never seen it. In terms of the light: that was not something I had planned for that shot. But to consider whether that is the reason I am using that take or not, I would say it’s not necessarily what I’m basing my decision on. In fact, if there’s anything within the image, it’s more about the fog that is in that shot, and also the performance that is there.

I think I in fact did do about ten takes, but not all from the same angle—we shot it from different angles at different positions. Ultimately I’m really looking at the positioning as well as the performance; those are the things that are really important to me. And the light that came in is something that I really noticed during the edit, and of course it’s not a bad thing to have because it certainly adds rhythm to the image. But fundamentally, I think what’s most important to me is the voice that is there: whether that voice is captured, and whether that voice that we captured is a good voice. That’s really what I based my decision of whether I used it or not.

And sometimes we do have these takes where the voice of the actor is a really good voice, but the image isn’t quite catching up to that level or quality. So there are times where we have actually replaced the voice of a good take over a different take. I’ve done that before, especially because of the reading process that we do where we do it over and over. It’s been possible for me to replace the voice in that way; sometimes it adds a certain kind of depth and heft to that moment, and density to that moment. I’ve done that quite a few times.

But in terms of what coincidence within the image is really important to me, first of all: it’s what coincidences are happening in the actors. And second is what’s going on in the background. The background stuff comes after the actors.
Have actors noticed when you swap audio between takes?
You know, I’ve never asked them, so I don’t know.
It certainly doesn’t feel like you’re using a worse take. So probably they wouldn’t complain.
[Laughs] I hope so.
Photo by Mettie Ostrowski, courtesy of the New York Film Festival.

In this film you have the young boy, Tomoki, who’s very autistic, and these older residents with some form of dementia—non-verbal, blank expressions. There’s a great dignity to how you portray these conditions. I’d like to know how you styled those performances so they feel real and dramatically potent, but not exploitative.

If that’s what it looks like to you, then I’m really glad to hear that because, ultimately, there’s not too much I can do, in the sense that everything we see in the film is a performance. So we’re doing something that is almost impossible, in the sense of: there’s just no way for it to be real. That’s true of all roles within the film—not just the people who are portrayed with dementia or autism. There’s an attitude that I have, which is to say: if it doesn’t work out or it doesn’t come across as real, that’s okay, because I’m attempting something that, ultimately, is impossible to achieve. But of course there’s the dignity of the actors who are performing these roles as well. I want to make sure that I create an environment where these characters can be seen and can be found through the performance.

Again: this isn’t limited to one role or another, but we tried to look at certain people within different contexts or different roles or different jobs. For example, regarding nurses: amongst every nurse, there’s different personalities. Each person has different backgrounds, different lives that have been lived. Of course we have to think about what kind of backgrounds or life these people have as individuals within this role as well. And during the reading process, I also try to make sure the actors have soaked in the words, assimilated with the words at a very physical, muscular level, and that’s sort of the process that I take with any role that I do. That’s true, also, of the role of somebody having dementia or somebody having autism as well. The person who portrayed Tomoki is Kodai Kurosaki, and what we had him do is go to some of these care facilities, go meet some of these people with autism, also talk to parents who have autistic children and had meetings with people and really ended up finding somebody who was a model of what he was portraying.

Another thing that we also did was read the book that has been translated into many languages, including English, which is The Reason I Jump by Naoki Higashida, who is somebody with autism who is able to write really well. That was definitely a reference point for us and Tomoki’s character, but again: with Tomoki’s character as well, I thought about what kind of history he has, what kind of relationships, backgrounds, what he likes and dislikes. All of these details are all things we all thought about. Tomoki’s character doesn’t have any dialogue, so our rehearsals were all about movement or how sounds were made.

Regarding the actors who portrayed people with dementia, again: it was a lot to do with observations of people with dementia, of seeing the way people move. But I also know it is really difficult for somebody who doesn’t have dementia to move in the same way. So what I ended up relying on was to say, “You don’t have to do anything extra. Don’t try to do too much.” Because the more you try to do, the more fake it starts to feel. For example, with one of my characters called Philippe Murano, we thought about his family background, the relationships that he has, and all these different things. So again: I’m not really categorizing these people as “this character has dementia” or “this character has autism,” but rather I’m just thinking about each individual’s life and thinking about each character, and really thinking about the process of what led them to this point. That’s something that I’m sharing with the actors, and the actors are really working to perform. The fact that you saw it this way makes me feel happy, but also feels really rewarding for all the effort that the performers put into it.
I had heard through the grapevine that you’re getting closer to making a film in America. You don’t have to tell me anything, but I’m intrigued, and if there’s anything you can or would say…

You know, after Drive My Car , I had people come up to me to ask whether I would be interested in shooting in the U.S. I would say filmmakers all over the world are thinking that, at one point, they would like to shoot something in the U.S. I’m certainly one of those people, too, but ultimately it’s about whether enough conditions are prepared for me to feel like I’m ready to do that—including my own language abilities or whether I have a certain project that’s been developed enough to feel ready in that way.

The answer to all that is: none of these are ready in that sense. Now that I’ve made this film in France, I feel like I’ve sort of got the confidence to know that, even if I’m directing a film in a foreign language or a foreign country, I can actually make decisions and I’m able to see when an actor is really concentrated or relaxed. Those things I can tell, even if it’s not my primary language, so if the opportunity comes, I’d like to dive into that.
Kiyoshi Kurosawa just told me he wants to make a film in New York, but if he couldn’t do that he’d shoot in Toronto and pretend it’s New York.
[Laughs]
I’ve said I might pass around a collection hat to get it made. Certainly I’d do the same for you.
Please! [Laughs]
Earlier this year I hosted a screening of Touching the Skin of Eeriness .
Oh, thank you.
Which I love. It’s great. And I forgot that the end says the story will be continued in a feature called Floods .
Yeah.
This never came to pass. Granted, it’s been a long time, but I don’t know if there’s any ambition to make a larger version.

I feel really bad for the actors because I’ve always wanted to make this sequel for sure, but it’s been 13 years now since I made that film, so I’m starting to run out of excuses, in a way. But at that time, I was thinking about this story, so it ends with the person taking themselves to the police and confessing, basically, so I always imagined the sequel to be after jail time and coming out of jail. So I figure that it’s okay if the character has aged in the sequel, so again: I’m constantly thinking of wanting to do a sequel. The actors in it were wonderful, and I would really love to work with them again in a proper way. But scriptwriting is really difficult; it’s really difficult to write an interesting script. It’s a mystery to me how a script ends up getting made. Sometimes I’m able to write something; sometimes it just doesn’t work out. So I just kind of have to ask my actors to wait.
You could also shoot it in America. Two birds, one stone.

[Laughs] You know, that’s really interesting, because with All of a Sudden , it wasn’t initially planned to be shot in France. It was when this conversation around France came up that suddenly a new path opened for me and made it possible to visualize this source material. So maybe the answer is something like that. [Laughs]
All of a Sudden opens in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.
